routes.description: Establish a physical resurrection as the historically reasonable explanation of Jesus's death, the early bodily-resurrection proclamation, reported individual and group encounters, and the claimed absence of his body.
routes.successCriteria: Connect testimony, bodily continuity, witness conduct, and the tomb into a coherent resurrection explanation while identifying relevant differences from rival miracle traditions and accounting for proposed natural alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined historical considerations make Jesus's physical resurrection a reasonable conclusion relative to the alternatives under discussion.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the earliest testimony and later narratives concern encounters with the physically continuous, crucified Jesus rather than only visions or disembodied survival.
Establish a historically usable missing-body or empty-tomb datum and explain why reburial, theft, or related burial hypotheses do not exhaust the combined evidence.
Connect individual and group encounter reports, conversions, and early proclamation to a single resurrection explanation of the movement's central claim.
Apply a consistent evidential framework to rival miracle claims while identifying differences relevant to testimony, incentives, expectations, corroboration, and background knowledge.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use danger, persistence, and costly proclamation to establish informed sincerity without treating suffering by itself as proof of resurrection.
Explain why admitting the possibility of supernatural events does not require endorsing every miracle report or its surrounding religious system.

routes.description: Show that the surviving evidence does not warrant concluding that Jesus physically rose because its bodily character, independence, corroboration, and comparative force remain uncertain and plausible alternatives persist.
routes.successCriteria: Demonstrate that visionary development, source limitations, natural tomb explanations, and comparable rival testimony prevent the cited considerations from specifically establishing a physical resurrection.

motionBridge.description: Show that the historical record does not make a physical resurrection sufficiently specific or warranted among the available explanations.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Pauline and Gospel materials do not unambiguously preserve firsthand testimony to ordinary physical encounters with the risen Jesus.
Provide historically plausible burial, reburial, theft, or narrative-development accounts that prevent a missing body from uniquely indicating resurrection.
Show that comparable miracle and witness traditions create a consistency test that the resurrection evidence must satisfy without selective standards.
Separate sincere belief, persecution, conversion, and visionary experience from firsthand knowledge of a physical resurrection and death specifically for that testimony.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify the absence or limits of independent, identifiable, and contemporaneous corroboration for the reported postmortem appearances.
Test whether the narrated burial authorization, tomb placement, and discovery details fit the relevant historical and narrative circumstances.

sections.title: Bodily Character and Development of the Appearance Traditions
sections.rationale: The motion requires a physical resurrection, so the meaning of Pauline bodily language, Gospel physicality, retained wounds, recognition scenes, and possible visionary development determines what event the sources purport to support.

sections.title: Appearances, Corroboration, and Explanatory Inference
sections.rationale: Individual and group encounter reports, the five hundred, Paul and James, companion corroboration, and the early proclamation form the principal testimonial basis for comparing resurrection with visionary or developmental explanations.

sections.title: Empty Tomb, Burial History, and Natural Alternatives
sections.rationale: The tomb is the principal proposed link between appearance testimony and a physically absent corpse, making burial plausibility, women witnesses, apologetic features, reburial, theft, and grave-disturbance alternatives burden-relevant.

sections.title: Rival Miracle Claims and Consistent Evidential Standards
sections.rationale: Mormon witnesses, Brigham Young's reported transfiguration, later Christian miracles, and possible non-Christian wonders test whether the historical criteria used for resurrection testimony distinguish it from structurally similar claims.

sections.title: Sincerity, Persecution, and Martyrdom Evidence
sections.rationale: Costly proclamation can bear on witness sincerity, but its force depends on the historical basis for apostolic danger or death and on whether the relevant people possessed firsthand bodily knowledge rather than visionary conviction.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Pauline and Gospel descriptions combine spiritual language and barrier-crossing or untouchable qualities with touching and eating, leaving the appearances ambiguous as evidence of an ordinary physical body.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Alex directly, and the ensuing sustained first-person skeptical response is clearly O'Connor's speech.

response.rationale: This is a constructive challenge to whether the cited sources unambiguously describe ordinary physical encounters; it establishes an ambiguity rather than answering an earlier locked move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops a central source-interpretation issue using several specified textual tensions.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ambiguity claim is recoverable and expressly qualified, though movement between Paul, 2 Peter, and Gospel scenes somewhat broadens the source scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues that the descriptions are ambiguous rather than claiming that physical resurrection is impossible, matching its mixed textual examples.

charity.alternative: A transformed physical body can possess unusual capacities while remaining bodily.
charity.decisiveQualification: Compatibility does not by itself remove the evidential ambiguity created by the differing descriptions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The contrasting descriptions coherently support ambiguity, with a bounded implicit bridge from unusual bodily properties to reduced evidential specificity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies Pauline language and concrete Gospel features, but compresses authorship, context, and the warrant for treating them as one evidential set.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It bears directly on the central skeptical requirement that the earliest and later sources remain ambiguous about ordinary physical encounters.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges the touching and eating material that favors physicality, although it does not fully develop the transformed-body synthesis.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt juxtaposes flesh-and-blood language, release from a bodily tent, movement through walls, and invitations to touch Jesus's feet.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Mormon witness traditions present collective testimony, continued attestation after estrangement, persecution, and disputed physical-versus-visionary experience, creating a consistency test for resurrection testimony.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly introduces Mormonism and develops the comparison continuously in his own voice across the entire source window.

response.rationale: This constructive comparison supplies a consistency test by identifying allegedly parallel collective testimony, estrangement, continued attestation, persecution, and ambiguity about visionary experience.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely establishes the major comparative issue governing rival-witness parity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is a clearly bounded consistency challenge, and it does not assert that the Mormon and resurrection traditions are identical in every respect.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparison is advanced as an evidential test and left-field parallel, not as certain disproof of resurrection testimony.

charity.alternative: Resurrection testimony may differ in incentives, historical setting, and the character of the reported event.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those differences must be shown to affect reliability rather than merely noting that the traditions are not identical.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy coherently shifts the burden toward identifying reliability-relevant differences, with only a bounded implicit assumption that the listed parallels matter comparably.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete witness features are supplied, but the historical documentation and independence of those features are compressed within the move.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move nearly maximizes central-tier relevance by directly constructing the rival-parity test required by the skeptical route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move poses a fair consistency challenge while leaving room for relevant disanalogies, though it does not anticipate each proposed distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source span introduces the three and eight Book of Mormon witnesses and develops collective attestation, estrangement, persecution, and physical-versus-visionary ambiguity.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Reports of Brigham Young's transfiguration contain more identifiable testimonial detail than Paul's unverified report of five hundred witnesses, whose identities, gathering, beliefs, and accessibility remain unknown.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted argument is delivered by O'Connor, who names historical Mormon reports and directly compares them with Pauline resurrection testimony.

response.rationale: This constructive move attacks the corroborative value of Paul's five-hundred report through missing identities, circumstances, accessibility, and verification, reinforced by a Mormon comparison.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives a focused and developed challenge to a principal claimed instance of group corroboration.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison and its verification deficits are specific and recoverable, with the conclusion limited to relative testimonial detail and corroborative force.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The specified verification gaps support skepticism, though relative detail alone does not establish that the Mormon report is evidentially stronger overall.

charity.alternative: Paul's invitation that surviving witnesses could be consulted may function as an early public verification gesture.
charity.decisiveQualification: The surviving text still does not identify the witnesses or independently document their experience and accessibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The missing verification details logically limit corroborative force, though the comparison with a later, more detailed report requires a bounded independence warrant.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It names dates, reports, and concrete verification deficits, while leaving the reliability and independence of the comparative Mormon sources partly compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is at the top of the subsidiary tier because it directly tests independent, identifiable, and contemporaneous corroboration for a major appearance report.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move engages the possible consultability of the witnesses and fairly explains why that feature does not amount to completed corroboration.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span contrasts dated Brigham Young transfiguration reports with Paul's five-hundred claim and questions witness identities, gathering circumstances, beliefs, and availability.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: Paul's Jewish framework and transformed-body language support physical resurrection rather than disembodied survival, while embodied Gospel encounters and an empty tomb distinguish resurrection from a vision.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests Horn's response, and Horn then gives a continuous first-person interpretation of Paul and resurrection experience.

components.text: Explain why Paul's spiritual and flesh-and-blood language does not make the risen body disembodied or evidentially ambiguous.
Account for the Gospel combination of unusual capacities with touching, eating, and an empty tomb.

response.rationale: The reply directly interprets Paul's language through a Jewish transformed-body framework and invokes eating and the empty tomb. It contacts both major components, although the barrier-crossing and untouchability examples receive less explicit reconciliation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a full answer within the repository class, but it falls below 90 because one group of cited Gospel tensions is only implicitly resolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The physical-resurrection interpretation is clear and stable, with a bounded implicit qualification that physical identity need not entail ordinary mortal bodily capacities.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited linguistic and narrative considerations strongly favor Horn's reading, but the move understates continuing interpretive uncertainty about Pauline terminology.

charity.alternative: Paul's spiritual-body and flesh-and-blood language could indicate a mode unlike ordinary corporeality.
charity.decisiveQualification: A transformed body can differ from mortal flesh while still being corporeal and continuous with the buried person.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Jewish resurrection expectations, transformed bodily continuity, eating, and the empty tomb form a coherent physicality inference with one bounded interpretive bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply uses specific Pauline language and Gospel actions, but its claims about Jewish expectations and the Semitism are asserted more than independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It sits at the top of the central tier because it directly advances the indispensable bodily-appearances bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the strongest semantic alternative directly and supplies the decisive transformed-body qualification, with only limited treatment of all Gospel anomalies.

moves.evidenceBasis: Horn cites eating fish, denial of being a ghost or spirit, Jewish resurrection expectations, the empty tomb, and a Semitic reading of flesh and blood.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: Christian theology can admit genuine post-apostolic or non-Christian wonders without thereby endorsing every doctrine of the religion surrounding such an event.
moves.attributionBasis: Horn explicitly labels the passage as his reply and speaks from a Catholic continuationist position throughout the complete argumentative unit.

components.text: Identify reliability-relevant differences that explain why comparable rival miracle testimony should receive a different evidential assessment.

response.rationale: Allowing genuine wonders outside Christianity answers a surrounding theological concern, but it does not assess the Mormon witnesses or supply the requested comparative reliability standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a relevant nonanswer within its class: it bears on rival miracles but leaves the decisive parity demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The narrow admissibility claim is clearly stated and expressly separates occurrence of a wonder from endorsement of the surrounding religion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move makes only a modal theological claim and provides a fitting illustration without inflating it into evidence that any particular wonder occurred.

charity.alternative: A miracle associated with another religion may count as evidence for that religion's truth claims.
charity.decisiveQualification: An isolated beneficial intervention need not endorse every doctrine or institutional claim associated with the beneficiary.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between permitting an event and endorsing an entire religious system is explicit, consistent, and illustrated by a clear example.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The theological compatibility claim is coherently illustrated, though the premise about divine action across religions is asserted rather than independently established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is highly relevant within the subsidiary tier because it directly advances the supernatural-prior bridge, despite not resolving central rival parity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately distinguishes an event's possible occurrence from wholesale doctrinal endorsement and preserves the evidential alternative in qualified form.

moves.evidenceBasis: Horn states that God could aid a non-Christian miraculously out of love without thereby affirming Buddhism or another surrounding theology.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: Mormon witness claims are distinguishable from resurrection testimony by prompting and investment among witnesses, Joseph Smith's worldly incentives, possible artifacts or hoaxes, and conflicts with established historical knowledge.
moves.attributionBasis: Horn enumerates the disanalogies in a continuous response, consistently referring to Mormon witnesses, Joseph Smith, apostles, and Christianity.

components.text: Provide reliability-relevant disanalogies between Mormon witness traditions and resurrection testimony under a consistent evidential standard.
Address the force of collective Mormon testimony despite estrangement and continued attestation.

response.rationale: The reply supplies several proposed disanalogies involving prompting, investment, incentives, possible artifacts or hoaxes, and conflict with background history. It does not squarely answer continued attestation after estrangement.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a high partial answer because it contacts the decisive comparative demand but leaves an important supporting parity component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The disanalogies are recoverable, but the move shifts among three witnesses, plates, Joseph Smith, and broader Mormon historical claims without always delimiting which witness claim each objection affects.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The proposed differences can lower comparative force, but some possibilities, especially artifact or hoax hypotheses, are not sufficiently established to carry the full conclusion.

charity.alternative: Estranged witnesses who continue affirming an experience may possess less institutional incentive and therefore stronger independence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Continued affirmation does not resolve prompting, interpretation, prior investment, or the reliability of the underlying object and event.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple disanalogies coherently weaken simple parity, but their cumulative inference is compressed and some objections apply to different Mormon claims.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Kinderhook plates, prompting, investment, and incentives are specific, yet documentation and the connection of each feature to witness unreliability remain materially compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central pro requirement to discriminate resurrection testimony from structurally similar rival traditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes several serious reliability dimensions but materially underdevelops the skeptic's strongest point about post-estrangement attestation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The reply cites possible natural artifacts and hoaxes, discrepancies and prompting among three witnesses, witness investment, Joseph Smith's incentives, and conflicts with historical knowledge.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Paul is unclear about the resurrected body's physicality, while later Gospel appearance accounts become increasingly elaborate and theological rather than supplying an unambiguous early bodily description.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator and interlocutor address Alex by name, and the uninterrupted first-person argument matches his skeptical position throughout the surrounding exchange.

components.text: Show that Paul's transformed-body terminology unambiguously supports corporeal continuity rather than an unclear spiritual mode.
Show that later embodied Gospel scenes independently resolve the ambiguity in Paul's earlier description.

response.rationale: The reply directly disputes the clarity of Paul's terminology and argues that later Gospel elaboration does not supply an unambiguous early bodily description. It contacts both components but gives limited source-development support.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a full answer within the class, though it remains below 90 because its development inference is more asserted than explicitly demonstrated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently distinguishes Paul's earlier ambiguity from the later and more elaborate Gospel descriptions, while expressly using cautious language.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling Paul at best unclear and proposing later elaboration is proportionate to the limited textual chronology offered in the span.

charity.alternative: Paul's transformed spiritual body can remain physical, and later Gospels can clarify rather than invent that meaning.
charity.decisiveQualification: That synthesis remains interpretive unless the earlier language itself clearly entails the later narratives' concrete physical features.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The chronology and increasing elaboration coherently preserve ambiguity, though the bridge from elaboration to theological development remains partly implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It engages Pauline and Gospel content specifically, but offers limited documentation for the claimed developmental pattern and its causal interpretation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central skeptical source-ambiguity bridge and attacks a principal proposed Pauline resolution.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply states Horn's transformed-body reading before explaining why it does not eliminate the earlier source ambiguity.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor expressly engages Horn's reading of spiritual body and Philippians, characterizes Paul as unclear, and contrasts that with increasingly elaborate Gospel accounts.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: Paul's bodily terminology indicates corporeality, and Jesus's retained crucifixion wounds identify the risen figure as the same embodied person who was crucified.
moves.attributionBasis: Trent explicitly turns to Alex's objection about Paul's bodily language and continues with his own interpretation of the wounds and personal identity.

components.text: Explain why the appearance traditions identify the risen figure as the same embodied Jesus rather than a duplicate or disembodied entity.
Show that bodily continuity is grounded in the relevant source descriptions rather than merely later theological elaboration.
Reconcile retained wounds with the spiritual, barrier-crossing, and untouchable features cited against ordinary physicality.

response.rationale: The retained-wounds argument directly contacts personal and bodily continuity, but it does not resolve the full inconsistency objection or establish that the wound tradition is early rather than developed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that contacts a decisive bodily-continuity component while leaving two important source and property challenges unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The continuity inference is clearly recoverable, with a bounded implicit assumption that retained wounds are evidentially historical rather than solely symbolic.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Retained wounds fit identity and continuity, but the move gives the theological motif more historical evidential force than its support alone establishes.

charity.alternative: Retained wounds may be a later literary or theological identity device rather than independent evidence of physical continuity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even as a theological motif, the wounds show that the narrative's claim concerns continuity with the crucified body.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Visible crucifixion wounds coherently identify the risen figure with the crucified person, subject to one bounded premise about the evidential status of the account.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The wounds are a specific source feature, but the argument leans on poetic theology and does not defend the account's date, independence, or historicity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the central bodily-appearances bridge by arguing for corporeality and identity continuity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move strongly addresses what the narratives purport to claim, but it does not fully answer the alternative about the tradition's historical development.

moves.evidenceBasis: Horn appeals to Paul's bodily terminology and especially to preserved crucifixion wounds as identifying Jesus as the same person, body and soul, who was crucified.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: Luke's historical reliability and relationship to Paul support reports of group appearances, while the limited period of appearances weighs against uncontrolled visionary enthusiasm.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained answer follows Trent's first-person transition to hallucination claims and includes an interlocutor's brief challenge before Trent resumes the same case.

components.text: Supply identifiable, independent, or otherwise verifiable corroboration for Paul's report that five hundred people saw Jesus.
Explain why Luke's later group-appearance narratives should be treated as reliable history rather than theological development.

response.rationale: The move offers Luke's reliability and connection to Paul as support for group appearances and limits visionary enthusiasm by the finite appearance period. It does not supply the missing verification details for the five hundred.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a relevant nonanswer near the top of that class because it offers adjacent group-source support but leaves the decisive five-hundred demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed support is recoverable, though Luke's general reliability, companionship with Paul, group appearances, and limited duration are compressed into a broad source inference.

calibrationFindings.rationale: General confidence in Luke and a limited appearance period do not by themselves establish independent group corroboration or defeat visionary explanations.

charity.alternative: Luke's group narratives may depend on Christian tradition and theological development rather than independent eyewitness corroboration.
charity.decisiveQualification: A source's general reliability and proximity to Paul do not establish independence for each particular appearance report.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from Luke's general reliability and relationship to Paul to particular group appearances leaves a material source-specific bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move substantially relies on asserted general reliability and companionship without representative verification of Luke's access, independence, or the five-hundred report.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances the testimonial-explanation bridge by defending group reports, though it misses the narrower corroboration demand.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the need to answer hallucination and development accounts but omits the decisive qualification concerning source independence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Horn invokes Luke as a reliable source, points to Luke's relationship with Paul and reports of group appearances, and argues that appearances ceased after a limited period.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: Danger faced by informed apostolic proclaimers supports the sincerity of their testimony, while Paul's conversion from hostile persecutor supplies a feature absent from the proposed Mormon parallel.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker states Trent's previously articulated distinction between dying for error and dying for a known lie, then develops his apostolic comparison after clarification.

components.text: Identify a sincerity- or incentive-relevant difference between early resurrection proclaimers and the proposed Mormon parallel.
Address Mormon witnesses who maintained testimony despite estrangement, persecution, or institutional cost.
Provide corroboration that the relevant apostolic proclaimers possessed firsthand knowledge of the reported group event.

response.rationale: The reply contacts comparative incentives through danger, lack of worldly reward, and Paul's hostile prior position. It does not address estranged Mormon attestation or establish firsthand access for all relevant proclaimers.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer: it contacts a significant comparative component but leaves other decisive parity and knowledge components unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The sincerity claim is expressly limited, but the move shifts from apostles generally to Paul specifically without fully specifying which people had what firsthand information.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Danger and hostile prior commitment can support sincerity, but the inference is somewhat stronger than the move's historical specification of danger and knowledge permits.

charity.alternative: Mormon witnesses also accepted costs and continued attesting after estrangement, while sincere danger does not establish physical truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: Paul's hostile prior position and the absence of an obvious worldly reward can still be relevant to sincerity without proving resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The limited inference from informed danger and hostile prior commitment to sincerity is coherent, with a bounded gap about which proclaimers were adequately informed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul's hostile prior position and claimed danger are concrete features, but generalized apostolic risk and lack of reward receive limited historical defense here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is highly relevant within the subsidiary sincerity tier because it expressly uses danger only to support informed sincerity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the distinction between sincerity and truth and supplies a relevant Pauline difference, while underaddressing costly Mormon attestation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Horn contrasts Joseph Smith's possible rewards with apostolic danger, treats martyrdom risk as evidence of sincerity, and highlights Paul's conversion from persecutor to proclaimer.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: Early indications of apostolic danger support sincere resurrection testimony without proving resurrection by themselves, and apocryphal reports should be assessed individually rather than accepted or rejected wholesale.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Trent to answer Alex, after which Trent restates his argument, cites early sources, and distinguishes his treatment of apocryphal evidence.

components.text: Whether early proclamation carried costs capable of supporting informed sincerity rather than opportunistic invention.

response.rationale: Horn directly argues that early proclaimers faced danger and would know whether they had fabricated the claim, while expressly limiting the inference to sincerity rather than resurrection truth. The excerpt does not directly resolve the bodily-development thesis, so contact is partial and issue-bearing.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that contacts a supporting sincerity issue but not the target's decisive source-development inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim clearly distinguishes evidence of risky proclamation and sincerity from proof that resurrection occurred, with apocryphal evidence treated case by case.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited sincerity inference is appropriately qualified, though the claim that early proclaimers would know fabrication compresses differences among transmitters and experiences.

charity.alternative: Costly proclamation may reflect sincere visionary belief rather than knowing fabrication of a bodily resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Danger supports sincerity only for people shown to possess relevant firsthand knowledge of the asserted event.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from knowingly risky proclamation to sincerity is coherent and expressly limited, with one bounded bridge concerning firsthand knowledge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move invokes early indications and Pauline danger but compresses documentation connecting particular proclaimers, knowledge, and resurrection-specific risk.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the subsidiary sincerity bridge while stopping short of making costly proclamation a central resurrection proof.

representationalCharity.rationale: Horn acknowledges that suffering does not itself prove resurrection, but only partly addresses the strongest visionary-belief qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Horn contrasts socially rewarded modern testimony with early proclaimers who faced danger, says they would know if the account were fabricated, and limits suffering to evidence of sincerity.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: The canonical tomb narratives appear sober compared with later embellishment, while their guards and socially disadvantageous women witnesses support an early historical empty-tomb tradition.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted argument precedes the moderator's direct invitation for Alex to answer Trent's women-witnesses argument.

components.text: Whether later narrative elaboration undermines the historical usability of the canonical physical and tomb traditions.

response.rationale: Horn answers the development concern by contrasting the canonical account's relative sobriety with later embellishment and adducing guards and socially disadvantageous women as signs of an early empty-tomb tradition. He does not independently establish every narrated detail.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive development concern but supplies only a compressed comparative and social-disadvantage warrant.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but 'sober' remains comparative and only implicitly specifies which canonical features and later accounts set the baseline.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Horn presents the features as support rather than certainty and concedes an apologetic explanation, but moves quickly from motifs to an empty-tomb inference.

charity.alternative: Guards and women could be literary or apologetic features within a developing narrative rather than historical residues.
charity.decisiveQualification: An apologetic motif can presuppose an empty-tomb claim without independently proving the underlying tomb was empty.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The combined sobriety and embarrassment inference is intelligible, but the move leaves a material bridge from narrative features to historical occurrence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific textual features are identified, yet their dating, independence, social force, and ability to establish an empty tomb are not defended in depth.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The argument directly supports the central empty-tomb bridge through the character and witnesses of the discovery narratives.

representationalCharity.rationale: Horn expressly entertains an invented apologetic motif, but his conclusion that it still shows emptiness compresses the distinction between narrative presupposition and history.

moves.evidenceBasis: Horn calls the account sober, notes the young man or angel, considers guards an apologetic motif that presupposes an empty tomb, and invokes women witnesses as socially disadvantageous testimony.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Evidence for Jesus before crucifixion has supportive and hostile extrabiblical corroboration, whereas the reported postmortem appearances, including the five hundred, lack comparable independent corroboration.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex directly rejects Trent's earlier equivalence claim and repeatedly distinguishes pre-crucifixion extrabiblical material from post-resurrection Christian testimony.

components.text: Whether Christian appearance reports provide corroboration comparable to the evidence establishing Jesus's pre-crucifixion existence.
Whether risky proclamation supplies independent corroboration of the reported postmortem appearances.

response.rationale: O'Connor expressly identifies the equivocation in treating pre-crucifixion and postmortem evidence as equally supported: the former has supportive and hostile extrabiblical material, while the latter remains within Christian testimony. That defeats the asserted evidential equivalence, though it does not answer sincerity from risk.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly identifies the failed comparison and states its consequence for independent corroboration of appearances.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast is clearly limited to comparative independent corroboration of pre-crucifixion existence and postmortem appearances.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative claim is well framed, but saying there is no extrabiblical material compresses questions about later non-Christian references and their evidential relevance.

charity.alternative: Early Christian sources can be historically probative even when no hostile or non-Christian source records the appearances.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument challenges parity and independence, not the possibility that insider testimony retains some historical value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidential comparison is explicit and consistently distinguishes existence evidence from evidence for postmortem appearances.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names a concrete source-category difference, though it does not catalogue the materials or fully analyze their independence and temporal proximity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the top of the subsidiary corroboration tier by directly challenging independent support for the appearance reports.

representationalCharity.rationale: O'Connor fairly allows Gospel testimony while explaining why it lacks the additional corroborative feature supporting Jesus's ordinary historical existence.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor concedes comparable Gospel testimony but says the historical-Jesus case gains strength from supportive and hostile extrabiblical material absent for post-resurrection appearances, including the five hundred.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: Resurrection provides a unified explanation for the conversions of the previously unbelieving James and hostile Paul and for the apostles' transition from fear to bold proclamation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker presents the pro-side explanatory inference in first person, and Alex's next turn directly addresses Trent by name in response.

components.text: Whether the resurrection inference has explanatory support despite the absence of comparable extrabiblical appearance corroboration.
Whether Paul and James can be explained without a bodily resurrection despite later narrative development.

response.rationale: Horn shifts from independent corroboration to explanatory breadth, citing James, Paul, and apostolic conduct as data jointly explained by resurrection. This contacts the skeptical demand but does not supply independent verification or compare developed natural explanations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive explanatory issue, but only partially answers the stated independence and source-development concerns.

precisionFindings.rationale: The unified-explanation proposition and its three data points are clear, with the comparative scope of 'much more difficult' left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move strongly favors resurrection without comparing conversion, visionary, social, or literary-development explanations for each cited datum.

charity.alternative: James's and Paul's conversions and later apostolic boldness could arise from sincere visions, group reinforcement, or developed tradition.
charity.decisiveQualification: A unified explanation gains force only after its likelihood and complexity are compared with those rival mechanisms.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A common-cause inference is coherent, but the move leaves the major bridge from conversions and boldness to specifically bodily resurrection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The compressed span asserts the conversions and behavioral transition without sourcing them or seriously comparing rival explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central testimonial-explanation bridge by offering resurrection as a unified account of conversions and conduct.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states that alternatives are harder but does not develop the strongest natural explanations or the decisive comparative qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Horn cites the conversions of previously unbelieving James and persecuting Paul, plus frightened apostles becoming bold proclaimers, and says resurrection explains this combined data well.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Persecution and martyrdom do not establish bodily resurrection where the clearest cases concern visions or the evidence does not show what the alleged witnesses saw and why they died.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex introduces the distinction after Trent's concession and develops it through Paul, Stephen, Peter and James before restating the required caution.

components.text: Whether apostolic persecution bears on firsthand knowledge of a bodily resurrection rather than sincere visionary conviction.
Whether Paul's conversion and later conduct specifically support a bodily encounter.

response.rationale: O'Connor expressly diagnoses the gap: Paul's well-attested persecution can establish commitment, but Paul's described experience is a light rather than meeting the bodily Jesus. He extends the distinction to uncertainty about what other alleged witnesses saw and why they died.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly identifies the inference's missing bodily-knowledge premise and states why persecution cannot supply it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently separates persecution, experience type, firsthand bodily knowledge, and the reason for an alleged martyr's death.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The negative conclusion is proportionate: the evidence does not establish the required link, rather than proving that no bodily encounter occurred.

charity.alternative: Paul's visionary encounter and apostolic suffering can still support sincere belief within a cumulative resurrection case.
charity.decisiveQualification: Sincerity and cumulative relevance do not independently establish firsthand perception of a physically risen body.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument explicitly distinguishes sincerity from bodily knowledge and death for a specific claim, resolving the central inferential challenge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It uses Paul's letters and the reported light experience specifically, though the broader Peter, Stephen, and James documentation remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central sincerity-gap bridge by separating costly commitment from relevant firsthand bodily knowledge.

representationalCharity.rationale: O'Connor grants Paul's persecution and targets only the stronger bodily-knowledge inference, accurately preserving the limited pro-side value.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor grants that Paul's letters clearly describe persecution but emphasizes that Paul's experience was a flash of light, then distinguishes uncertain witness experience and reasons for death.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A temporarily used emergency tomb followed by proper reburial or grave robbery provides historically plausible natural explanations for an empty tomb without uniquely indicating resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex explicitly returns to the empty-tomb question and develops a sustained skeptical scenario until the moderator gives Trent time to answer those claims.

components.text: Whether an empty tomb, even if historically granted, specifically indicates resurrection rather than relocation or theft.
Whether the broader appearance and conversion data eliminate natural missing-body accounts.

response.rationale: O'Connor directly supplies two natural empty-tomb mechanisms: temporary emergency placement followed by reburial, and grave robbery. Mary's initial inference that the body was taken is used as narrative compatibility, but the move does not answer the separate appearance evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive empty-tomb specificity demand is contacted, while the cumulative appearance component remains unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly presents reburial and theft as plausible hypotheses preventing uniqueness, not as established historical facts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The stated force is appropriately modal and the move distinguishes two hypotheses without asserting that either certainly occurred.

charity.alternative: An intact missing body, burial goods, appearances, and early proclamation may make ordinary grave robbery or unnoticed reburial comparatively strained.
charity.decisiveQualification: Natural possibilities must be compared with the full conjunction of tomb and appearance evidence, not merely shown compatible with emptiness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternatives validly defeat uniqueness if sufficiently plausible, with one bounded missing bridge concerning access, timing, and later discovery.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The emergency-tomb scenario, Mary's inference, and ancient body theft are specific, but historical frequency and case-specific feasibility remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central tomb-alternatives bridge with concrete reburial and theft hypotheses.

representationalCharity.rationale: O'Connor gives historically intelligible alternatives but does not fully engage the cumulative evidential conjunction that could reduce their comparative force.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor proposes temporary emergency placement followed by proper burial, notes that Mary initially assumes removal, and cites evidence that bodies were stolen in antiquity.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.proposition: Non-resurrection accounts require a conjunction of missing-body and appearance hypotheses, while grave robbery fits poorly with preserved burial goods and an intact missing body.
moves.attributionBasis: After the moderator requests Trent's response, Trent directly contrasts resurrection with skeptical hypotheses and continues through the delivered discussion of burial plausibility.

components.text: Whether reburial or theft plausibly explains an intact missing body together with the reported appearances.
Whether the appearance evidence has sufficient independent corroboration to form the proposed conjunction.

response.rationale: Horn directly argues that skeptical accounts require multiple hypotheses and specifically challenges grave robbery because valuables, rather than intact bodies, were typical targets. He does not resolve the independence of appearance reports or fully analyze reburial.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the principal alternatives and cumulative-fit demand but leaves corroboration and the reburial branch materially underanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conjunction objection is clear, but 'the data' and which natural accounts necessarily require independent hypotheses are only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Multiple auxiliary hypotheses can lower probability, but that consequence depends on independence and prior plausibility, which the move does not establish.

charity.alternative: A single developmental or social process could generate appearance reports while an ordinary burial event explains the missing body without an exceptionally costly conjunction.
charity.decisiveQualification: Counting hypotheses is probative only after their dependence, priors, and fit are compared with the resurrection hypothesis's own assumptions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative inference is usable, but it leaves material assumptions about hypothesis independence and the resurrection account's own complexity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The valuables-based robbery distinction is specific, yet the preservation of burial goods, intact-body pattern, and reburial comparison are insufficiently documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central tomb-alternatives bridge by challenging cumulative fit and the grave-robbery mechanism.

representationalCharity.rationale: Horn recognizes concrete theft evidence but portrays skeptical accounts as compounded without fully addressing unified or dependent natural alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Horn argues that combining separate missing-body and appearance hypotheses lowers probability, says alternatives compress data, and distinguishes valuables-seeking grave robbery from removal of an intact body.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The Gospel portrayal of Pilate compassionately authorizing Jesus's burial is historically questionable because other accounts characterize Pilate as a ruthless ruler.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly presents first-person historical skepticism characteristic of O'Connor's position and follows Horn's burial explanation.

components.text: Whether grave robbery and reburial fit the combined missing-body and appearance evidence better than resurrection.
Whether the Gospel burial and tomb narrative is historically reliable given its portrayal of Pilate.

response.rationale: The brief reply challenges the Gospel characterization of Pilate and therefore bears on antecedent burial plausibility, but it does not contact Horn's decisive conjunction or grave-robbery inference. It is relevant contrary material rather than an answer to the immediately selected demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This relevant nonanswer materially bears on burial history but leaves the primary conjunction argument untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical challenge is clear, though the inference from general ruthlessness to this particular authorization relies on an implicit contextual qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A ruthless general character does not by itself make a pragmatic or customary burial authorization unlikely without further institutional context.

charity.alternative: A ruthless governor could authorize burial for pragmatic, customary, or order-preserving reasons without compassion for Jesus.
charity.decisiveQualification: The Gospel's compassionate characterization and the bare fact of authorization are distinct historical claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The character-based challenge is relevant but leaves a substantial unsupported conditional from ruthlessness to denial of burial authorization.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move asserts Pilate's ruthlessness without identifying the comparative accounts or evidence governing burial decisions in this case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It substantially advances the subsidiary burial-plausibility bridge by questioning a prerequisite to the narrated tomb placement.

representationalCharity.rationale: O'Connor presses the characterization of Pilate but does not preserve the strongest non-compassionate explanation of the authorization itself.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor contrasts the Gospels' compassionate Pilate with his understanding of Pilate as ruthless and indifferent, using that contrast to question the burial portrayal.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A witness who retains an extraordinary-experience claim while repudiating its associated religious institution may offer unusually independent testimony rather than thereby weakening the claim.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker develops a skeptical alternative explanation and a hypothetical involving Paul that aligns with O'Connor's comparative argument.

components.text: Whether estrangement from Mormon institutions weakens continued witness attestation through loss of group alignment.

response.rationale: O'Connor expressly reverses Horn's inference: retaining an extraordinary-experience claim while repudiating its institutional interpretation can reduce an alignment incentive and therefore strengthen independence. The hypothetical Paul reversal states the defeating comparative consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly identifies why defection need not weaken testimony and articulates the opposite evidential consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The independence claim is clear and confined to retained testimony after institutional repudiation, with reliability implications appropriately implicit rather than universal.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hesitant framing presents a plausible counter-inference rather than claiming that every defector is independent or reliable.

charity.alternative: A defector may retain a face-saving supernatural claim, so continued attestation after estrangement need not be independent evidence of the original event.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reduced institutional loyalty removes one incentive but does not remove reputational, identity, memory, or interpretive incentives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counter-inference from repudiation plus retained testimony to reduced institutional dependence is coherent, with a bounded incentive-analysis gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers a useful Paul hypothetical but little concrete examination of the defectors' statements, incentives, or evidential independence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central rival-parity bridge by defending the comparative force of estranged Mormon witnesses.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reverse-pull insight fairly answers group alignment, though it omits several remaining incentives that limit the independence inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor argues that repudiating a religious institution while retaining the original extraordinary claim creates a reverse pull, illustrated by imagining Paul abandoning Christianity but maintaining his experience.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: The historical case lacks the combined evidence of identifiable firsthand testimony to a bodily risen Jesus and martyrdom specifically for that resurrection testimony rather than for Christian affiliation generally.
moves.attributionBasis: The extended first-person answer states O'Connor's evidential standard and explains why the evidence discussed does not meet it.

components.text: Whether danger and martyrdom concern identifiable firsthand bodily witnesses and the resurrection claim specifically.
Whether conversion and bold proclamation supply the missing firsthand bodily testimony.

response.rationale: O'Connor justifies a more exact evidential demand that preserves the sincerity issue: identify firsthand bodily testimony, establish persecution or martyrdom of those witnesses, and connect the cost specifically to resurrection testimony rather than Christian affiliation. He then says the discussed evidence lacks that conjunction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe explicitly preserves legitimate sincerity evidence while specifying and applying the missing knowledge-and-causation requirements.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition distinctly specifies identifiable apostles, firsthand bodily experience, supported persecution or martyrdom, and resurrection-specific causation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move states an evidential deficit and a conditional standard rather than claiming certainty that no such witness or martyr existed.

charity.alternative: General persecution and early willingness to proclaim can still raise sincerity even when resurrection-specific martyrdom documentation is incomplete.
charity.decisiveQualification: That limited sincerity increment does not establish firsthand bodily knowledge or death specifically for refusing to recant it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument cleanly separates testimony, firsthand bodily content, persecution evidence, and resurrection-specific causation without equivocation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evidential standard is well defended by the inference it tests, though the excerpt does not exhaustively document each apostle's source record.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the top of the central sincerity-gap tier by specifying precisely why the combined martyrdom inference remains incomplete.

representationalCharity.rationale: O'Connor preserves the limited value of costly affiliation while accurately identifying what is needed for the stronger testimonial inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor requires firsthand testimony to bodily encounters plus good evidence that those same apostles were persecuted or martyred specifically for resurrection belief, not merely Christian identity or preaching.
